 He Owed the IRS $48,000 From a 2013 Audit and Could Only Ever Send Them $200 a Month. In 2024 the Ten-Year Clock Ran Out, and the Rest of the Debt Stopped Existing
 The IRS has a collection deadline most taxpayers never hear about, and missing it can change everything about a debt that seemed impossible to escape.
 By David Beren 
 Published October 18, 2026, 4:19pm ET · 4 min read 
 Life After Work desk. Editor: David Beren .
 𝕏 
 f 
 ⧉ 
 Quick Read
 The IRS has a 10-year collection window on tax debt; once it closes, any unpaid balance legally stops existing and cannot be pursued.
 A $200/month payment on a $48,000 audit debt wiped out the remaining balance in 2024 when the 10-year clock expired.
 Bankruptcy, living abroad, or submitting an offer in compromise can pause the clock and push the expiration date further out.

 Federal tax debt carries an expiration date, and anyone with an IRS balance they cannot fully repay has a stake in it. Under the IRS 10-year statute of limitations on collection, the agency generally has 10 years from the date it assesses a tax to collect it, plus penalties and interest.
 Once that window closes, the agency generally can no longer collect the unpaid remainder. The headline case centered on a $48,000 balance from a 2013 audit, paid at $200 a month, that became uncollectible once the clock ran out in 2024.
 How a Tax Debt Runs Out of Time
 The IRS tracks this deadline as the Collection Statute Expiration Date, or CSED, and each assessment starts its own clock, so an audit adjustment posted years after the original return gets a separate 10-year window measured from the audit assessment. Payments under an installment agreement reduce the balance over time, but they don’t change the expiration date.
 If monthly payments are too small to pay off the debt before the CSED, the IRS can still approve the plan as a partial-payment installment agreement. Any balance left at expiration generally can no longer be collected.
 Where the Ten-Year Limit Is Written Into Federal Law
 The rule sits in 26 U.S.C. § 6502(a)(1). It lets the IRS collect by levy or court proceeding only if that action begins “within 10 years after the assessment of the tax”. The authority for plans that never cover the full amount comes from 26 U.S.C. § 6159(a), which permits installment agreements that “facilitate full or partial collection” of a liability.
 The IRS’s Internal Revenue Manual states that a partial-payment installment agreement may be used if taxpayers cannot make full payment by the Collection Statute Expiration Date. The statute’s current text keeps this 10-year structure in place for 2026.
 Who Gets Relief and Who Gets Left Out
 The rule helps taxpayers with an assessed federal balance and too little income to pay it off before the deadline, and it does nothing for people who never filed a return because the § 6502 clock starts only after an assessment exists.
 It also gives limited relief to taxpayers who can afford to pay in full, since partial plans are meant for cases where full payment cannot happen by the CSED. Interest and penalties also keep accruing on unpaid tax even if the IRS grants your request for an installment plan. So the balance can grow even as you pay it down.
 How Taxpayers Can Find and Protect Their Expiration Date
 Taxpayers can pull an account transcript through their IRS online account or with Form 4506-T, and note the assessment date for each tax year and each audit adjustment.
 Taxpayers who cannot pay in full can request a payment plan online at IRS.gov/OPA or with Form 9465. A partial payment agreement is an option when full payment does not fit a taxpayer’s finances.
 An installment agreement depends on on-time payments. If the IRS ends an agreement, it can levy after a 30-day window, unless the taxpayer files an appeal within that window.
 Requesting an extension of the deadline affects the collection period. Under § 6502(a)(2)(A), a written extension agreed to when you set up an installment agreement keeps the debt collectible until 90 days after the agreed period ends.
 Events That Pause the Clock and Push Back the Expiration Date
 Several events stop the 10-year clock , and each delay pushes the end date back. A bankruptcy case suspends the collection period while the IRS is blocked from collecting, plus 6 months thereafter, under §6503(h). Living outside the United States for at least 6 months suspends the clock during that absence under §6503(c).
 Requesting a Collection Due Process hearing pauses the clock. While the hearing and any appeals are pending, the period cannot expire before the 90th day after a final determination, under §6330(e)(1).
 A pending offer in compromise or a pending installment agreement request also stops the clock, along with the 30 days after any rejection, through §6331(k) and §6331(i)(5). The statute exempts an installment agreement already in effect from that suspension under §6331(k)(3)(B). That exemption is what lets the clock keep running while a taxpayer makes steady payments under an approved plan.
 The IRS also has one path around the deadline. If it files a timely lawsuit to collect, §6502(a) lets collection continue until the liability or the resulting judgment “is satisfied or becomes unenforceable”. The IRS’s Publication 594 covers collection rights, liens, and levies. Each tax year’s transcript shows the assessment date that starts its own clock.
